lesson.lo: compare and group materials as solids, liquids or gases using their observable properties
lesson.tib: I understand how the three states of matter help scientists explain how most substances in the world around us behave
lesson.isb: creating a sorting table with at least six materials correctly grouped and one written reason for each

slides.title: What do you already know about materials?
bullets: Think about the objects around you — how would you describe them?
Which materials can you pour? Which ones keep their shape?
Do you know what the words solid, liquid and gas mean?

slides.title: Sort these — solid, liquid or gas?
How are the particles arranged?
bullets: In a SOLID, particles are packed tightly in a fixed arrangement — the solid keeps its shape.
In a LIQUID, particles are close but can slide past each other — the liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
In a GAS, particles move quickly and are spread far apart — the gas fills the entire space available.

slides.title: Is this a solid or a liquid?
Sort the materials
bullets: Sort the material cards into three groups: solid, liquid or gas
Record your decisions in the table on your LP
For each material, write one reason — use the particle model to help you
Challenge: can you find one material that is difficult to classify? Why?

slides.title: Who do you agree with and why?

learners.name: Learner A
learners.statement: Sand is a liquid — you can pour it from one container to another, just like water.

learners.name: Learner B
learners.statement: Sand is a solid, but when there are lots of grains together they can act a bit like a liquid.

learners.name: Learner C
learners.statement: Each grain of sand is a solid. Even when you pour sand, every single grain keeps its own shape.

starters: I can now explain the difference between a solid, liquid and gas because…
